slides.text:
Employee attrition rate
A wonderful company with a healthy and thriving culture set in a
scenic country setting had experienced alarming levels of attrition
• It is not just the HR but also the fellow employees who noticed it
• The HR goes to a statistician and gives her the data for all the
employees who worked at the company
• The data was fed into a model by the statistician, and she came up
with all the fancy numbers and charts
• The conclusion reached from her exercise was that employees
below the age of 30 who live 20+ miles from work do not stay for
long

• Examples:
• Statistical analysis
• Forecasting models
• Linear programming
• Decision theory
• Simulation

slides.text:
Statistics
Statistics is derived from the Italian word stato, which means ‘state’
▪ Statista refers to a person involved with the affairs of the ‘state’
▪ Statistics originally meant the ‘collection of facts’ useful to the statista
▪ Today, Statistics as a terminology has moved beyond affairs of the
state to every state of human endeavor –personal, business, social,
environmental or so on.
▪ Has moved beyond the focus on data collection towards summarizing,
displaying and analyzing data into meaningful information thereby
facilitating current and future decisions.

Scenario
A telephone survey was conducted for the Florida Department of Tourism (www.myflorida.com) to
gain an understanding of the travel behavior of in-state residents. In 2008, there were more than 18
million residents in Florida, ranking the state fourth in the United States after California, Texas, and
New York. These households were stratified by north, central, and south Florida regions. A
computerized random digit sample was used to reach these households.
• Households were screened to locate family members who met four qualifications: 1. Age 25 or older
2. Live in Florida at least seven months of the year 3. Have lived in Florida for at least two years 4.
Have a Florida driver’s license
• To obtain a representative sample of qualified individuals, a random method was used to select the
respondent from within a household. All household members meeting the four qualifications were
listed and the person with the next birthday was selected. Repeated callbacks were made to reach

slides.text:
Scenario
The steps in the sampling design process were as follows:
1. Target population: Adults meeting the four qualifications (element) in a household with a working
telephone number (sampling unit) in the state of Florida (extent) during the survey period (time)
2. Sampling frame: Computer program for generating random telephone numbers
3. Sampling technique: Stratified sampling. The target population was geographically stratified into
three regions: north, central, and south Florida.
4. Sample size: 868
5. Execution: Allocate the sample among strata; use computerized random digit dialing; list all the
members in the household who meet the four qualifications; select one member of the household
using the next birthday method

Sampling Types
Probability Sampling: A Technique in which all the eligible individuals
have an equal chance of getting selected in the sample from the whole
sample space. More time-consuming and expensive. Guarantees that the
sample is representative of the population.
• Non-Probability Sampling: A Technique in which the researcher selects
the sample based on subjective judgment rather than random selection.

slides.visual_text: Heading: Sampling Types. Probability Sampling Methods: Simple Random Sampling: random selection of 200 students from a school having 2000 students; assign a number from 1 to 2000 to each student; use a random number generator to generate 200 random numbers between 1 and 2000 and select the corresponding students. Systematic Sampling: to select 25 students from a school of 500 students, sorted in alphabetical order of first name; randomly selected the starting number and picked the first student on that number; subsequently selected every Nth student from the first selection onwards; N is calculated by dividing the total number of students by the required number. Stratified Sampling: population divided into groups and then proportionate numbers are selected randomly from each group; India population is divided into N, S, W, E regions; N, S, W, E have 100, 200, 300, 400 million people respectively; to get a sample of 100 people, 10, 20, 30 and 40 people are selected randomly from N, S, W, E respectively. Clustered Sampling: data is divided into clusters based upon certain characteristics; randomly, clusters are selected from the available list of clusters; a school has 15 branches in India, randomly 5 branches are selected for sample; TIET has 10 departments, select 3 out of 10 randomly. Non-Probability Sampling Methods: Convenience Sampling: samples are selected from the population directly because they are conveniently available for the researcher; samples are easy to select, and the researcher did not choose the sample that outlines the entire population. Consecutive Sampling: similar to convenience sampling, the difference being that the researcher picks a single person or group of people for sampling, analyzes that particular sample and then selects a further sample as needed. Quota Sampling: sample generalizes the entire population in scope by picking individuals based on specific traits or qualities. Judgment / Purposive Sampling: sample is selected based upon the researcher's knowledge or judgement. Snowball Sampling: also known as chain-referral sampling, where referred sample members are asked to recommend further sample elements.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text: Summary
slides.visual_text: Heading: Summary. A table of Technique, Strengths, Weaknesses. Nonprobability sampling: Convenience sampling: least expensive, least time-consuming, most convenient / selection bias, sample not representative, not recommended for descriptive or causal research. Judgmental sampling: low cost, convenient, not time-consuming / does not allow generalization, subjective. Quota sampling: sample can be controlled for certain characteristics / selection bias, no assurance of representativeness. Snowball sampling: can estimate rare characteristics / time-consuming. Probability sampling: Simple random sampling (SRS): easily understood, results projectable / difficult to construct sampling frame, expensive, lower precision, no assurance of representativeness. Systematic sampling: can increase representativeness, easier to implement than SRS, sampling frame not necessary / can decrease representativeness if there are cyclical patterns. Stratified sampling: includes all important subpopulations, precision / difficult to select relevant stratification variables, not feasible to stratify on many variables, expensive. Cluster sampling: easy to implement, cost-effective / imprecise, difficult to compute and interpret results.

What is a scale?
Scaling involves creating a continuum upon which measured objects are located. Scaling may be
considered an extension of measurement.
• Consider a scale from 1 to 100 for locating consumers according to the characteristic “attitude
toward department stores.” Each respondent is assigned a number from 1 to 100 indicating the
degree of (un)favorable ness, with 1 = extremely unfavorable, and 100 = extremely favorable
• Measurement is the actual assignment of a number from 1 to 100 to each respondent. Scaling is
the process of placing the respondents on a continuum with respect to their attitude toward
department stores. | ay be

• Interval- Equal Intervals, Magnitude (or) Rank and Identity (or) Category.
• Ratio –Absolute Zero, Equal Intervals, Magnitude and Identity (or) Category.

slides.visual_text: Heading: Scales of Measurement. Bullets: Nominal: Identity (or) Category. Ordinal: Magnitude (or) Rank and Identity (or) Category. Interval: Equal Intervals, Magnitude (or) Rank and Identity (or) Category. Ratio: Absolute Zero, Equal Intervals, Magnitude and Identity (or) Category. A table of Type of Scale, Characteristics of Data, Basic Empirical Operation, Example. Nominal: classification (mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive categories), but no order, distance, or natural origin; determination of equality; gender (male, female). Ordinal: classification and order, but no distance or natural origin; determination of greater or lesser value; doneness of meat (well, medium well, medium rare, rare). Interval: classification, order, and distance, but no natural origin; determination of equality of intervals or differences; temperature in degrees. Ratio: classification, order, distance, and natural origin; determination of equality of ratios; age in years.
